Analysis

Can the Mac Studio M2 Ultra 64GB Run DeepSeek R1 14B at Q8_0 — the detailed answer

The Mac Studio M2 Ultra 64GB provides 64 GB of unified memory, of which about 46.1 GB is realistically usable by DeepSeek R1 14B. It combines 64 GB of unified memory with 800 GB/s of bandwidth, nearly three times the Mac Mini M4 Pro's ceiling. Short answer for DeepSeek R1 14B at Q8_0 on the Mac Studio M2 Ultra 64GB: yes, comfortably. At Q8_0 (8.50 bits per weight) its weights occupy 14.6 GB, and a 16K-token context adds 3.00 GB of KV cache, for roughly 19.1 GB including the 1.5 GB runtime reserve. That leaves 26.9 GB of headroom, so the whole model stays in unified memory and even the full 128K native context window fits. Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, so expect roughly 30 tokens per second, which feels comfortably interactive. There is enough spare memory to step up to FP16 / BF16 for slightly better fidelity. Usable memory is still capped near 46 GB after macOS takes its share, so its capacity matches the Mac Mini while its speed does not. As a platform for local step-by-step reasoning for coding and analysis, call it a genuinely responsive setup.

Reference

How local LLM memory math works

Running a model locally is a memory problem before it is a compute problem. Three numbers decide whether a model fits: the size of the quantized weights, the KV cache that grows with context length, and a fixed runtime reserve for activations, the CUDA context and the display. Get those three right and the rest of the configuration follows.

1. Model weights

Weight memory is a direct multiplication of parameter count and precision:

weights_GB = params × bits_per_weight / 8 / 1024³

7B × 4.83 bits ≈ 4.2 GB  |  70B × 4.83 bits ≈ 42.2 GB

The nominal label is not the real number. "Q4_K_M" is a 4-bit scheme, but the effective average is about 4.83 bits per weight because each block of 32 weights stores scale and minimum values in higher precision. That overhead is why a 70B Q4 model is 42 GB rather than the 35 GB a naive 4-bit division suggests. The table below lists the effective bits per weight for the GGUF quantizations you will actually encounter.

GGUF quantization levels, effective bits per weight and quality impact
QuantBits/weightQualityWhen to use
FP16 / BF1616.00LosslessFull-precision weights. Reference quality, 2× the memory of Q8.
Q8_08.50Indistinguishable8-bit near-lossless; the safe choice when memory allows.
Q6_K6.56ExcellentRarely worth it over Q5_K_M unless you have spare VRAM.
Q5_K_M5.67Very goodSweet spot for long-context work where quality matters.
Q4_K_M4.83GoodDefault community choice; best size/quality trade-off.
IQ3_XS3.30DegradedAggressive 3-bit; expect visible degradation on small models.
2-bit (Q2_K)2.60PoorLast resort for squeezing a large model into small memory.

2. The KV cache is the hidden cost

Every generated token needs the attention keys and values of all previous tokens. That cache is held in memory for the whole session and scales linearly with context length:

kv_GB = 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_element × tokens / 1024³

70B, 80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dim, FP16: 0.3125 MB / token → 2.5 GB at 8K, 40 GB at 128K

Two modern techniques keep this manageable. Grouped-query attention (GQA) reduces KV heads from the full attention-head count — often 64 down to 8 — cutting the cache by eight times. KV cache quantization stores the cache at 8 bits instead of 16, halving it again with almost no measurable quality loss. Together they turn a 40 GB cache into about 2.5 GB, which is why a 128K-context model can fit on a 24 GB card at all.

Note that long-reasoning models read the same math differently: a chain-of-thought trace of 20,000 tokens occupies cache as surely as a 20,000-token prompt. Budgeting context for a reasoning model means budgeting for its thinking, not just its input.

3. Runtime overhead and usable memory

A model never gets the whole card. The graphics driver, the CUDA context, attention workspace and the compositor on a desktop system consume roughly 1–2 GB before inference starts. On Windows with a browser open it is usually worse. We reserve a flat 1.5 GB, and we apply a usable-memory ratio — 90% on consumer GPUs, 95% on workstation cards, and 70–72% on Apple silicon, where macOS itself needs headroom to stay responsive.

This is the difference between "the math says 24 GB" and "it runs". A 70B Q4 model at 42 GB is not going to fit on a 48 GB card with a 32K context even though 42 is less than 48, because the cache and reserve add another 12 GB.

4. Speed comes from memory bandwidth

Token generation is memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. To emit one token, the GPU must read every active weight once. Theoretical throughput is therefore bandwidth divided by bytes read per token:

tokens_per_sec ≈ bandwidth_GB/s ÷ weights_GB

RTX 4090 (1008 GB/s) with 8B Q4 (4.8 GB) ≈ 210 tok/s theoretical, ~40–70 measured

Real throughput lands at 40–70% of the theoretical ceiling because of kernel launch overhead, prompt processing, sampling and batch effects. This is why an RTX 5090 with 32 GB and 1792 GB/s is the strongest single-card option: it wins on both capacity and bandwidth at once. It is also why a 192 GB Mac Studio, with only about 819 GB/s, feels slow despite its enormous capacity.

When a model does not fit, llama.cpp offloads layers to system RAM and streams them over PCIe. Throughput collapses to single digits, because PCIe offers 16–64 GB/s against a GPU's 500–3000 GB/s. Partial offload is a way to run a model you cannot otherwise load — not a way to run it well.

5. Practical sizing rules

  • 8 GB runs 3B–8B at Q4 with a modest context; good for autocomplete and small assistants.
  • 12–16 GB is the 8B sweet spot, or 14B at Q4 with 8K context.
  • 24 GB comfortably runs 32B at Q4 with 16K context — the best quality-per-dollar tier today.
  • 48 GB (dual 24 GB or one workstation card) reaches 70B at Q4 with a short context.
  • 80 GB+ handles 70B at Q8 or 120B-class MoE at Q4 with real context for serving.
  • Every doubling of context roughly doubles KV cache; check that before buying a bigger model.

Methodology and limitations

Weight estimates use effective bits per weight for GGUF quantization plus a 3% uplift for mixture-of-experts checkpoints, which carry router and shared-expert tensors on top of the nominal parameter count. KV cache uses GQA-aware layer and head counts matched to the nearest known architecture profile — if your model is not in the table, a custom parameter count is interpolated to the closest profile and can be off by 20–30%. Speed estimates assume single-stream decoding with full GPU offload. Actual performance depends on your runtime, batch size, power limits and driver version. Treat every number as a planning estimate, not a benchmark.
